blocks.text: Violetta’s Bed-room—at the back a Bed, with the curtains partly drawn—A window shut in by inside shutters—Near the bed a stool with a bottle of water, a crystal cup, and different kinds of medicine on it—In the middle of the room a toilet-table and settee; a little apart from which is another piece of furniture, upon which a night-lamp is burning—On the left a fire-place with a fire in it.
Violetta discovered sleeping on the Bed—Annina, seated near the fire-place, has fallen asleep.

lines: Oh! see you that it is daylight?

blocks.text: Opens the shutters, and looks into the street.

lines: I wish to rise—pray help me.

blocks.text: She rises, but falls again—then, supported by Annina, she walks slowly toward the settee, and the Doctor enters in time to assist her to sit upon it—Annina places cushions about her.

lines: How very good to think of me so early!
How do you feel yourself now?
Suffering in body, but my mind is tranquil.
A clergyman came to me and gave me comfort.
Ah! there’s nothing like religion for a wounded spirit!
Convalescence can not be far distant.
Well, farewell—by and by I’ll see you again.

blocks.text: In a low tone, whilst following the Doctor.

lines: A few hours, and Death will surely claim her.
All Paris the fool is playing—’tis the Carnival.
Ah! in this general joy, Heaven only knows
See what money is in the cupboard.
Take ten of them, and amongst the poor disburse them.
Go and fetch me my letters.
Oh, I’ve no wants; yet be not long returning.

blocks.text: Violetta, who takes a letter from her bosom, and reads.

lines: The Baron is wounded, but is now better.
And your sacrifice I myself revealed.
Get well, you have deserved a better fate.
I wait and wait, but they come—

blocks.text: Looks at herself in the glass.

lines: But the Doctor bade me still to keep on hoping—
Ah! such diseases leave naught but death to hope for.
Adieu! thou art fled, the bright dream of my childhood;
The rose from my cheek is fast fading away;
The friend of my bosom is willing to fly me,
And thoughts of the loved one but bring me dismay.
Oh! list to a truly unfortunate’s prayer!
Oh! grant her thy pity—sustain and forgive.
Yes, soon will my joys and my troubles be ended;
The broken in heart in the grave may find rest;
No tear may bedew me, nor floweret bestrew me,
Nor cross with my name spread its arms o’er my breast.
Oh! list to a truly unfortunate’s prayer!
Oh! grant her thy pity—sustain and forgive!
For all will soon be o’er.
This wondrous ox of wondrous size.
And gay boys shall greet him,
This wondrous ox of wondrous size.
To-day, now, you’re better—do you not feel better?
To be calm, will you promise?
Ah! Alfred! Hast thou seen him! has he arrived! Oh! urge him!

blocks.text: Annina makes signs with her hand in the affirmative, and goes to open the door.
Alfred enters, pale with emotion, and they throw themselves into each other’s arms, exclaiming—

lines: Oh! I am guilty; I know all, dear one.
I, too, know, thou art restored to me.
This beating heart will tell how much I love thee.
I could no longer live, dear one, without thee.
And if thou find’st me still alive,
Believe that grief has not the power to kill
Forget the pain—O much adored one!
Have I the power? ’Tis I am guilty;
But love it was that made me so.
Nor man nor demon dearest love,
Shall have the power to make us part.
Come, then, from Paris, oh! let us be flying,
We’ll live united in love undying.
Thou’lt be rewarded for sadness and gloom—
There in thy beauty again thou wilt bloom.
Life, love and light wilt thou be to me,
And all the future happy shall be.
Come, then, from Paris, oh! let us be flying,
We’ll live united in love undying.
Thou’lt be rewarded for sadness and gloom—
Health, love and light wilt thou be to me,
And all future happy shall be.
Ah! no more! To the temple, O Alfred! let us go,
Our thanks for your return to render.
Can never enter a troubled bosom without a pain.

blocks.text: She sinks on a chair fainting, and her head falls backwards.

lines: It is the nature of this sad illness
’Tis nothing! Annina, my dress bring hither.
But not now? Oh! wait love.

blocks.text: Annina presents the dress, which she makes an effort to put on, but finds she is too weak, and exclaims—
She throws away the dress vexedly, and sinks again on the chair.

lines: Ah! tell him—say that Alfred has now returned—
Oh, yes! returned to love, and me—
Tell him I wish again to live—for him I wish to live anew—
But, if thy coming back cannot save me,
No power on earth can ever do so.
Great Heaven! ’tis sad that hope should fail
But sadder still, that after all
My pain, I thus should die.
And all my constancy and truth
O Alfred! what a cruel ending to all our love.
O beauteous being! light and life,
And all my heart holds dear,
If thou art sad, I, too, must weep—
My heaven on earth is here!
But oh! when all my strength I need,
Ah! tell me not that hope is dead,
O Violetta! calm thyself—’tis death thy grief to see!

blocks.text: The same, Germont and the Doctor.

lines: And come to press you to my bosom
Grenville, bear witness, in the midst I’m dying
Of all to me who’re dearest.
Dost see her, O my father!
E’en now my soul is torn by deep remorse.
Every word she speaks like a thunderbolt shakes me.
Dost see the mischief thou has done?

blocks.text: Having opened a drawer over her toilette-table, she takes out a medallion, and says—

lines: Approach me nearer. Oh! cherish, dearest Alfred,
Of myself, in days since faded.
’Twill serve to remind thee of one
If a virgin, pure and true,
Thou in the flower of youth should’st meet.
Who to thee her heart would give,
Ah! espouse and love her well—I wish it,
Tell her that she who gave it thee
Thou shalt not die! Ah! say not so,
But live for love and me!
Ah! live! or else one coffin
Oh! noble victim of a generous feeling,
While I have tears to weep,
They shall be shed for thee!
He claims thee as His own.
I have again returned to life!

blocks.text: She falls back again on the sofa.
A Tableau, and the curtain falls.
